moneySources: Frankfurt coin dealing and court-agent business

records.scaleNote: Rothschild & Co, controlled by the family holding Concordia, reported 2025 revenue of €2,986m and €143bn of client assets under management (Rothschild & Co Annual Review 2025).
records.lifespan: c. 1760 (Frankfurt) – present; London house from 1809, Paris from 1817
records.origins: Mayer Amschel Rothschild (1744–1812) rose from coin dealer in the Frankfurt Judengasse to court agent for the Landgrave (later Elector) of Hesse-Kassel. He sent his five sons to Frankfurt, London, Paris, Vienna and Naples, creating a multinational partnership that could move money across borders faster than governments could.
records.role_summary: The fortune was built by financing states. In 1814 the British commissary-in-chief J.C. Herries commissioned Nathan Mayer Rothschild to gather gold on the Continent for Wellington's army, a contract Nathan called 'the best business I ever did'; after 1815 the brothers dominated issuance of European sovereign bonds. Commissions on loans and bullion, interest, and exchange arbitrage across five houses compounded; in 1875 Lionel de Rothschild advanced £4m to the British government to buy the Khedive's Suez Canal shares, and in 1887 Natty Rothschild backed Cecil Rhodes's De Beers amalgamation.

roleDetail.d: Mayer Amschel's capital came from coin dealing and agency work for Hesse-Kassel, whose Elector was one of the richest princes of the era.
On receiving the commission from Herries in January 1814, Nathan had his brothers buy gold quietly in small lots across the Continent and convey it to Wellington in southern France.
The Rothschild Archive and the Fondation Napoléon both say the evidence that Nathan made a fortune from early news of Waterloo is slender; the legend originated in hostile pamphlets.
N M Rothschild & Sons advanced £4m to Disraeli's government to buy 176,602 Suez Canal Company shares from the Khedive of Egypt, charging a commission of 2.5% and 5% interest.
In 1887 Natty Rothschild backed De Beers' bid for the French Diamond Company, a step towards the 1888 creation of De Beers Consolidated Mines; Natty was later Rhodes's executor.

records.legacy: The English and French banking houses were merged into Rothschild & Co (Paris), which the family holding company Rothschild & Co Concordia took private in 2023, valuing the group at about €3.7bn. A separate Geneva group, Edmond de Rothschild, is run by Ariane de Rothschild. Family branches also own Bordeaux estates (Domaines Barons de Rothschild – Lafite), and charities such as the Rothschild Foundation (Waddesdon) and Yad Hanadiv in Israel.

legacyDetail.d: Concordia held 38.9% of capital, and the family concert 54.5% of capital and 66.8% of votes, before its 2023 offer at €48 a share (City A.M.); a squeeze-out at €38.60 ex-distribution followed.

Domaines Barons de Rothschild (Lafite), chaired by Saskia de Rothschild since 2018, owns about 1,200 ha of vineyards; the Rothschild Foundation, endowed by the late 4th Lord Rothschild, runs the Waddesdon estate for the National Trust.

records.name: Fugger family (Fugger von der Lilie; Princes Fugger-Babenhausen and Counts Fugger)
moneySources: Loans to the Habsburgs secured on mines
records.scaleNote: At peak (1520s) the firm financed most of the 1519 imperial election, 543,385 of about 851,585 guilders (Swiss National Museum). Today the family's visible assets are its foundations, its forests and seats; the 'Fugger' bank is 99% insurer-owned.
records.origins: Hans Fugger, a weaver, moved to Augsburg in 1367 and traded fustian. His grandson Jakob Fugger 'the Rich' (1459–1525) turned the firm into a lender to princes. He took mining revenues as security.
records.role_summary: From 1487 the Fuggers lent to Archduke Sigismund of Tyrol against shares in Tyrolean silver and copper output, then to Maximilian I. From 1495 they leased and built up the Neusohl copper mines in Hungary (Banská Bystrica) with Johann Thurzo. When Maximilian died in 1519 owing about 350,000 guilders, Jakob put up 543,385 of the roughly 851,585 guilders paid to the electors to make Charles V emperor, and was repaid in mining rights and revenue assignments.

roleDetail.d: The first loan to Archduke Sigismund was secured on an interest in the Schwaz silver and copper mines, which made the firm a metal trader as well as a lender.
With the mining expert Johann Thurzo, Jakob leased the Neusohl mines and built them into the leading copper centre of the age.
Fugger supplied about two-thirds of the election money for Charles V. The Welsers and three Italian firms supplied the rest.
The firm handled transfers to the Curia, including indulgence proceeds of the 1510s, which Luther attacked.
Repeated Spanish crown bankruptcies in the late 16th century left the firm with unrecoverable claims. The family then converted its money into land and titles.

records.legacy: The fortune survives mainly as land, seats and foundations. The Fürstlich und Gräflich Fuggersche Stiftungen still run the Fuggerei, founded in 1521, where annual rent remains one Rhenish guilder (€0.88). They are financed mainly by forestry. The Fürst Fugger Privatbank carries the name but has been 99% owned by the Nürnberger insurance group since 1998, with 1% in family hands.

legacyDetail.d: Since the late 1800s the foundations have been financed primarily by forestry income. Forests at Laugna, Bocksberg and Emersacker have been managed for over 200 years.

Börsen-Zeitung (Jan 2025): Nürnberger has owned 99% since 1998. Client assets exceed €7bn. In March 2026 Bloomberg Línea reported that Vienna Insurance Group, which is buying Nürnberger, was preparing a possible sale of the bank, citing unnamed sources; no decision had been made.

wealth.publishedNote: No current Forbes, Bloomberg or Manager Magazin figure for the Fugger family was found. Popular claims that Jakob Fugger was the 'richest man in history' are retrospective estimates, not filings.

grossAssets.text: No consolidated accounts are published for the family lines or the foundations. The Fürst Fugger Privatbank published key figures for 2025; in March 2026 Bloomberg, citing unnamed sources, reported that Vienna Insurance Group (which is acquiring the bank's owner, Nürnberger) was considering a sale, with one source putting the value at about €120m; no decision had been announced. This is not family property.

records.name: Medici family (Medici Bank; Grand Dukes of Tuscany)
moneySources: Bills of exchange across a branch network
Political rule of Florence and Tuscany
records.scaleNote: In the early 15th century the Rome branch, serving the papal court, produced more than half of the Medici Bank's profits (de Roover's figures, as summarised by Wikipedia and Brewminate).
records.origins: Giovanni di Bicci de' Medici separated his bank from his relative's Roman business in 1397 and moved its seat to Florence. Over long years in Rome he had built close ties to the papal Curia.
records.role_summary: The Medici became depositaries of the Apostolic Chamber. Papal revenues collected across Europe flowed through their branches as bills of exchange, giving them cheap deposits and fees. Branches in Rome, Venice, Geneva/Lyon, Bruges, London and Avignon lent to merchants and princes. Cosimo and Lorenzo converted bank profits into control of Florence, and later Medici became popes and Grand Dukes.

roleDetail.d: Holy See deposits gave the bank capital to invest elsewhere. The Rome branch produced over 50% of profits early in the century, by some counts up to 62%.

roleDetail.t: Bills of exchange avoided usury bans.
roleDetail.d: Profits were earned on exchange transactions between branches rather than on openly charged interest.

roleDetail.t: Loans to princes broke the branches.
roleDetail.d: Bad loans, including to rulers through the London and Bruges branches, weak management and poor coordination contributed to the collapse.
Piero de' Medici's exile during the French invasion precipitated the closure of the remaining branches.

records.legacy: No Medici banking capital survives. The lasting asset is cultural. By the Family Pact of 31 October 1737, Anna Maria Luisa de' Medici, the last of the line, left the dynasty's collections to the new Lorraine rulers on condition that nothing leave Florence. Those collections form the basis of the Uffizi and Pitti holdings.

legacyDetail.d: The 1737 Family Pact, confirmed in her will of 1739, took effect on her death in 1743.

wealth.publishedNote: The family line is extinct (1737/1743). No modern wealth figure exists, and claims by people with the Medici surname are not documented descent from the banking line.
wealth.gapNote: The Medici fortune is now public patrimony: the collections are owned by the Italian state, not by heirs.

records.name: Bardi and Peruzzi companies (Florence)
moneySources: Loans to Edward III secured on wool and customs
records.scaleNote: They were the largest of the medieval 'super-companies'. The chronicler Villani put Edward III's debts at about 900,000 florins to the Bardi and 600,000 to the Peruzzi, though Hunt argues the Peruzzi never had that much capital.
records.origins: Both Florentine merchant families built international companies trading grain, wool and cloth. They also handled papal and Angevin Neapolitan finances in the early 14th century.
records.role_summary: From the 1330s the Bardi and Peruzzi lent heavily to Edward III of England to fund his wars in Scotland and France. They took grants of wool and assignments of customs and taxes as repayment. Loans in 1338–39 exhausted both firms. When repayment faltered and the Florentine and Neapolitan economies turned, the Peruzzi failed in 1343 and the Bardi in 1346.

roleDetail.d: Repayment came as wool export licences and customs assignments, which tied the firms to English royal policy.
Britannica: those loans 'exhausted both Peruzzi and Bardi resources'.

roleDetail.t: Default was only part of the story.
roleDetail.d: Hunt (1990, 1994) argues that Edward's default was too small to explain the collapse alone. Losses in Naples and Florence and a credit squeeze also mattered, and Edward repaid part in cash and wool.

records.legacy: The companies were liquidated. The Bardi family survived as Florentine nobility and later invested in Iberian voyages, but no continuous fortune survives. The episode is the classic warning on sovereign lending.

legacyDetail.d: No company, foundation or estate can be traced from the super-companies to today.

wealth.publishedNote: Defunct since the 1340s. No modern figure exists.

records.name: Wallenberg family (Investor AB, SEB, Wallenberg Foundations)
moneySources: Industrial rescues and conversions of bank loans into equity
records.scaleNote: Investor AB, which the Wallenberg foundations control with 50% of the votes, reported adjusted net asset value of SEK 1,258.0bn at 30 September 2026.
records.origins: André Oscar Wallenberg (1816–1886), a naval officer and son of the Bishop of Linköping, founded Stockholms Enskilda Bank in 1856. The bank merged in 1972 into SEB.
records.role_summary: The Wallenbergs made their money as bankers who became owners. Enskilda Bank lent to Swedish industry and, in crises, took equity in borrowers such as Atlas, ASEA and Ericsson. Banking law later separated banks from industrial shareholdings, so in 1916 the family founded Investor to hold them. From 1917 Knut Wallenberg began moving the family's own wealth into foundations. The result is a fortune the family controls rather than owns: the three largest foundations hold 23.3% of Investor's capital and 50% of its votes.

roleDetail.d: Stockholms Enskilda Bank financed railways and industry and later merged into SEB (1972).
Rescues of indebted industrial clients left the bank holding shares. Investor (1916) was created to hold such stakes.
Knut and Alice Wallenberg set up their foundation in 1917. There are now 16 Wallenberg foundations, which granted SEK 3.1bn to Swedish research and education in 2025.
A shares carry more votes than B shares. That is how 23.3% of capital becomes 50% of votes at Investor.
The family co-founded EQT in 1994. In October 2026 Investor bought 12.5m EQT shares (SEK 3.5bn) from Wallenberg Investments, taking it to 14.98%.

records.name: Baring family (Baring Brothers & Co.)
records.scaleNote: At peak Barings channelled about £140m of investment to Argentina in 1885–90 (Bank Underground). In 1995 £827m of trading losses destroyed the bank and ING bought it for £1.
records.origins: Johann Baring, a Bremen cloth merchant, settled in Exeter. His sons John and Francis founded the London house in 1762, which grew from trade finance into a lender to governments.
records.role_summary: Barings earned commissions and discounts by buying government bonds and reselling them to investors. In 1803 Barings and Hope & Co bought the $11.25m of 6% US bonds that paid France for Louisiana at a 13.3% discount (FF52m for FF60m of bonds), roughly FF8m or $1.5m of discount in total. After 1815 they financed France's war indemnity. Over-exposure to Argentina forced the Bank of England's 1890 rescue. In 1995 unauthorised trading by Nick Leeson in Singapore caused £827m of losses.

roleDetail.d: On Louisiana the bankers bought at a discount and sold 'at or above par', keeping much of the spread (Baring Archive).
Unsold Argentine bonds froze Barings' capital. The Bank of England organised a £17m guarantee fund and split the firm into a good bank and a bad bank.
Profits bought estates and five peerages (Ashburton, Northbrook, Revelstoke, Cromer, Howick). Alexander Baring became Lord Ashburton in 1835.
Leeson's hidden error account 88888 ran up £827m of losses, about twice Barings' trading capital. ING bought the group for £1.

records.legacy: The family no longer owns a bank. ING absorbed Barings in 1995; the asset-management arm was later sold and now trades as Barings under MassMutual, an unrelated owner. The Baring Foundation (1969) became independent after the collapse, and its endowment came from the separate Manor Park Charitable Trust. The Baring Archive preserves the records.

legacyDetail.d: The Baring Foundation has given over £120m in grants since 1969. ING donated services and office space after 1995.

legacyDetail.t: Family wealth now private and dispersed.

records.name: Pictet and Lombard Odier (Geneva partner banks)
records.scaleNote: Pictet held CHF 757bn of assets under management or custody at end-2025. Lombard Odier reported CHF 349bn of client assets (CHF 367bn at mid-2026).
records.origins: Lombard Odier traces itself to Henri Hentsch's firm of 11 January 1796, joined by Jean-Gédéon Lombard in 1798. The Lombard, Odier, Darier and Hentsch families were Huguenot or Genevan settlers. Pictet descends from De Candolle, Mallet & Cie, founded in Geneva on 23 July 1805.
records.role_summary: Both houses earn fees on client assets: management and custody fees, brokerage and, later, institutional asset management. For two centuries their managing partners carried unlimited personal liability, and that personal guarantee was itself the selling point. Swiss banking secrecy drew foreign wealth into the business. When US enforcement ended the model, Pictet paid $122.9m under a 2023 deferred-prosecution agreement over 1,637 undeclared US accounts, and Lombard Odier paid $99.8m in 2015 under the DOJ Swiss Bank Program.

roleDetail.d: Until 1 January 2014 both firms were partnerships whose partners were personally liable without limit. Both then converted to corporate partnership forms.
Pictet's 2025 operating income was CHF 3.21bn and profit CHF 667m. Lombard Odier's net profit was CHF 200m on operating income of CHF 1,394m.

Banque Pictet admitted conspiring with US taxpayers to evade about $50.6m in US taxes in 2008–14 and paid $122,959,391 under its December 2023 DPA. Lombard Odier paid $99.8m under a 2015 non-prosecution agreement in the DOJ Swiss Bank Program.

On 27 July 2026 the Swiss Federal Criminal Court fined the bank Lombard Odier CHF 3m for lacking adequate organisational measures to prevent money laundering of funds linked to Gulnara Karimova; a former client manager received a suspended sentence for aggravated money laundering. The judgment is not final: the bank said it would appeal. No partner-family member was charged.

records.legacy: Ownership remains with a small group of managing partners: seven at Pictet, led by senior partner Marc Pictet, and six at Lombard Odier, led by Hubert Keller. Partners hold the equity and pass it on in batches every five to ten years. They are not all members of founding families.

legacyDetail.d: Pictet's ownership passes among owner-managers every five to ten years. The senior partner chairs the partners' meetings.

records.name: East India Company (English, later British)
moneySources: Royal monopoly charter on Asian trade (1600)
records.scaleNote: From 1765 the Company collected the land revenue of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa for a fixed tribute of 26 lakh rupees a year to the Mughal emperor (Banglapedia).
records.base: East India House, Leadenhall Street, London
records.origins: London merchants obtained a royal charter on 31 December 1600 granting a monopoly of English trade east of the Cape of Good Hope. Shareholders funded voyages for pepper, then Indian cloth.
records.role_summary: The Company began as a chartered trader and became a territorial power. After Plassey (1757), a firman of 12 August 1765 gave it the diwani, the right to collect revenue, of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. Bengal's taxes then paid for the goods it exported, replacing bullion shipped from Britain, and for its army. Servants who made private fortunes returned as 'nabobs' and bought estates and parliamentary seats. After it lost its trading functions in 1833, shareholders received a fixed 10.5% dividend charged on Indian revenues until 1874, when the stock was redeemed at £200 per £100.

roleDetail.d: Before 1765 the Company paid for Indian goods with silver and gold from Britain. Afterwards Bengal's revenue financed the 'investment' in exports.
Returned servants used fortunes to buy estates and seats in Parliament. Their numbers rose from about 12 MPs in 1761 to nearly 30 by 1780.
Parliament lent to the Company in its 1772–73 crisis in exchange for regulatory control (Regulating Act 1773).

roleDetail.t: A guaranteed dividend paid by Indian taxpayers.
roleDetail.d: Under the 1833 Act the Company's stock paid £10 10s a year. The 1873 Redemption Act paid it off on 30 April 1874 at £200 per £100 of stock, a cost charged to India.

records.legacy: The Company was dissolved in 1874 after the Crown took over its government in 1858. Its capital dispersed into the stock-holders' redemption money, nabob estates in Britain, and London banks and agency houses. No continuing corporate successor exists; a modern retailer bought the trade name.

legacyDetail.d: Holders received £200 per £100 of stock in 1874. The Viceroy estimated the redemption would save India £450,000 a year (Hansard, 1873).
Clive and others converted Indian fortunes into English land and political influence.

records.name: Hanseatic League (incl. the London Steelyard)
records.description: The Hanseatic League was a league of North German and Baltic merchant towns led by Lübeck that dominated northern European trade from the 13th to the 16th century. Its London Kontor, the Steelyard beside the Thames, was formally established in 1320 and exported English wool and later cloth. Lübeck, Bremen and Hamburg sold the Steelyard site to the South Eastern Railway in 1852, and Cannon Street station now stands on it.

records.name: Dutch West India Company (WIC / GWC)
records.description: The States-General chartered the Dutch West India Company on 3 June 1621 with a monopoly that included the Dutch Atlantic slave trade, Brazil, the Caribbean and North America. Its aim was economic warfare against Spain and Portugal. A reorganised company chartered in 1675 relied heavily on the slave trade and shipped about 187,000 enslaved Africans between 1674 and 1739. The state took it over in 1791.

records.name: Bank of England
records.description: The Bank of England was chartered on 27 July 1694 when 1,268 subscribers lent £1.2m to William III's government for the war against France. In return the Bank gained a charter and note-issuing rights. It was a private joint-stock company until it was nationalised in 1946. In 1890 it organised a £17m guarantee fund to rescue Barings, an early lender-of-last-resort operation.

records.name: South Sea Company (and the 1720 Bubble)
records.description: The South Sea Company was founded in 1711 to trade, mainly in enslaved Africans, with Spanish America. It took over government debt in exchange for its shares and received the asiento slave-trading contract in 1713 under the Treaty of Utrecht. Its 1720 scheme to absorb the national debt inflated a share bubble that collapsed from September 1720 and ruined many investors. Parliament passed the Bubble Act the same year.

records.name: City of London Corporation (and City's Estate / City's Cash)
records.description: The City of London Corporation is the municipal authority of the Square Mile, governed by the Court of Common Council, the Court of Aldermen and the Livery through Common Hall. Its private endowment, City's Cash (renamed City's Estate in 2023–24), dates from the 15th century and was built from property, bequests and statutory transfers. Its value has been reported at about £2.3bn (net assets, 2016) to about £2.7–2.8bn in later council papers.

records.name: Imperial election of Charles V (1519)
records.description: When Maximilian I died in 1519 owing Jakob Fugger about 350,000 guilders, Charles of Habsburg won the electors' votes with payments of about 851,585 guilders. Fugger supplied 543,385, about two-thirds. The Welsers and three Italian firms supplied the rest. Repayment came as mining rights and revenue assignments, and for the Welsers the Venezuela charter of 1528.

Lionel de Rothschild's terms were a 2.5% commission plus 5% interest. Parliament later voted the money to repay the loan.

records.name: Edward III's war loans and the Florentine bank failures (1338–1346)
records.description: Edward III borrowed heavily from the Bardi and Peruzzi to fund the opening of the Hundred Years' War, repaying in wool grants and customs assignments. The 1338–39 loans exhausted both firms. Villani's figures for the debts were 900,000 florins to the Bardi and 600,000 to the Peruzzi. The Peruzzi failed in 1343 and the Bardi in 1346, though Hunt argues the default was only one cause.

events.title: Peruzzi company fails; Bardi follow in 1346
events.text: After Edward III's war loans of 1338–39 exhausted both Florentine super-companies, the Peruzzi went bankrupt in 1343 and the Bardi in 1346. Historians now treat the royal default as one cause among several.

The family now controls €143bn of client assets while published family fortunes are a few billion at most.
